key_terms.meaning: R = ct/2; 1 µs of delay is 150 m
ΔR = cτ/2 for a pulse of width τ, or c/(2B) for a compressed pulse or FMCW sweep of bandwidth B
synchronizer → modulator → transmitter → duplexer → antenna; echo: antenna → duplexer → receiver → signal processor → display
S<sub>min</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>BF·(S/N)<sub>min</sub>, the noise floor times the S/N needed for detection
R<sub>max</sub> = [P<sub>t</sub>G²λ²σ/((4π)³S<sub>min</sub>L)]<sup>1/4</sup>; 16 times the power doubles it
σ = 4πR²S<sub>s</sub>/S<sub>i</sub>, an equivalent area in m² (dBsm = 10 log<sub>10</sub> σ)
Rayleigh σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴; optical σ = πa² (ka > 10); flat plate face-on σ = 4πA²/λ²
R<sub>unamb</sub> = c/(2·PRF); duty cycle τ·PRF; P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>τ·PRF
shown at R − nR<sub>unamb</sub>; resolved with two or more PRFs
f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ, positive for a closing target
v<sub>b</sub> = nλ·PRF/2; staggered PRF in ratio a/b raises the first one (a + b)/2 times
Σ = A + B + C + D, Δ<sub>az</sub> = (A + B) − (C + D), Δ<sub>el</sub> = (A + C) − (B + D); θ = (Δ/Σ)/k
P<sub>fa</sub> = (1 + α/N)<sup>−N</sup>; threshold αZ from N training cells
I = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(P<sub>t</sub>/P<sub>safe</sub>) dB; minimum range c(τ + t<sub>rec</sub>)/2

takeaways: A radar makes one basic measurement, the echo delay, which gives range as R = ct/2; the antenna angle gives direction and the Doppler shift gives radial speed.
Echo power falls as 1/R⁴, so range grows only as the fourth root of power, gain squared, σ and 1/S<sub>min</sub>: 16 times the power doubles the range.
The minimum detectable signal is the noise floor kT<sub>0</sub>BF times the S/N that detection needs; integrating pulses lowers the S/N needed per pulse.
Radar cross section is an equivalent area set by shape, aspect and wavelength, not the physical size: a face-on plate returns far more than a sphere of the same area.
The PRF fixes the unambiguous range c/(2·PRF) and the Doppler coverage, so low PRF suits search and high PRF suits fast targets; several PRFs remove both ambiguities.
A CW radar measures only speed; an FMCW sweep adds range from the beat frequency, and a triangular sweep separates range and Doppler.
MTI cancels fixed clutter by comparing pulses, at the price of blind speeds nλ·PRF/2; staggered PRF pushes them out, and pulse Doppler filter banks also measure speed.
Tracking radars need an error signal that is zero on boresight; monopulse forms it as Δ/Σ from one pulse, so echo fluctuation cannot disturb it.
The matched filter gives the best peak S/N, 2E/N<sub>0</sub>, for a known pulse; CFAR keeps the false-alarm rate fixed as the background changes.
Real radars build the block diagram from dish or array antennas, magnetron, klystron, TWT or solid-state transmitters, superheterodyne receivers and TR-tube or circulator duplexers.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the pulse radar block diagram with the job of each block, the derivation of the range equation, and short numerical problems on unambiguous range, Doppler shift, FMCW beat frequency and MTI blind speeds; tracking and detection questions want a labelled sketch and a comparison.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a pulse radar and explain the function of each block. For a radar with a 2 µs pulse at a PRF of 500 Hz and 250 kW peak power, state the timing and power figures that the synchronizer and modulator set.
outline: Block diagram with the transmit path and the echo path through the duplexer
Jobs of the synchronizer, modulator, transmitter, duplexer, antenna, receiver, processor and display
Numbers: T<sub>r</sub> = 2 ms, R<sub>unamb</sub> = 300 km, duty 0.001, P<sub>av</sub> = 250 W, ΔR = 300 m
Range measured from the synchronizer trigger, R = ct/2

answer.text: Block diagram (transmit path across the top, echo path back through the duplexer):
answer.pre:
Synchronizer ──trigger──► Modulator ──HV pulse──► Transmitter ──► Duplexer ◄──► Antenna
     │                                                      │
     └──── range zero ────► Display ◄── Signal processor ◄── Receiver

answer: Synchronizer (timer): the master clock. It fixes the PRF, triggers the modulator once per interval and starts the range count on the display and processor at the moment the pulse leaves, so that an echo at delay t is placed at R = ct/2.

Modulator: the high-voltage pulse generator. In a line-type modulator a pulse-forming network is charged between pulses and discharged through a switch into the transmitter tube, which conducts for exactly τ.
Transmitter: a magnetron (oscillator) or a klystron, TWT or solid-state amplifier chain that produces the high-power RF pulse.
Duplexer: TR and ATR tubes or a circulator with a limiter. It sends the pulse to the antenna and shields the receiver during transmission, then connects the antenna to the receiver between pulses.
Antenna: a reflector or array that forms a narrow beam, gives the gain G of the range equation and scans in azimuth (and elevation), so its pointing angle gives the target direction.
Receiver: a superheterodyne (LNA, mixer with STALO, IF amplifier near the matched-filter bandwidth 1/τ, detector). Its noise figure sets the minimum detectable signal.
Signal processor: MTI or Doppler filtering to remove clutter, and a CFAR threshold for the target/no-target decision.
Display: a PPI showing each target at its range and bearing, or target reports to a computer.

answer.text: Figures set by the synchronizer and modulator for the given radar:

answer: The transmitter and duplexer must survive 250 kW peak, but the power supply and cooling handle only 250 W on average, because the transmitter is on for one thousandth of the time.

Closing check: an echo at the edge of the unambiguous range returns after 2 × 300 000/3 × 10⁸ = 2 ms, exactly one interval, just before the next pulse; and 300 m resolution means two aircraft on the same bearing closer than 300 m in range merge into one echo.

bank.q: Derive the radar range equation for a monostatic radar, including the minimum detectable signal and system losses. Hence show how the maximum range depends on transmitter power, antenna gain, wavelength and target cross section, and find R<sub>max</sub> for P<sub>t</sub> = 250 kW, G = 36 dB, f = 5.6 GHz, σ = 5 m², B = 1 MHz, F = 3 dB, (S/N)<sub>min</sub> = 12 dB and L = 5 dB.
outline: Power density P<sub>t</sub>G/(4πR²) at the target
Power reradiated σ × density; echo density at the radar over 4πR² again
Received power with A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/(4π): P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G²λ²σ/((4π)³R⁴)
S<sub>min</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>BF(S/N)<sub>min</sub>; losses L; R<sub>max</sub> = [ … ]<sup>1/4</sup>
Fourth-root dependence and its consequences
Numerical: S<sub>min</sub> = 1.27 × 10⁻¹³ W, R<sub>max</sub> = 92.0 km
answer: Isotropic density: a transmitter of power P<sub>t</sub> radiating equally in all directions gives P<sub>t</sub>/(4πR²) W/m² at range R, the power spread over a sphere.
Directive antenna: the gain G concentrates this in the beam, so on the axis S<sub>i</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>G/(4πR²).
Target: by the definition of radar cross section, the target intercepts S<sub>i</sub>σ watts and reradiates it as if equally in all directions.
Echo density back at the radar: S<sub>s</sub> = S<sub>i</sub>σ/(4πR²) = P<sub>t</sub>Gσ/((4π)²R⁴).

Received power: the antenna collects S<sub>s</sub> over its effective aperture A<sub>e</sub>, so P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>GσA<sub>e</sub>/((4π)²R⁴). Using A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/(4π) for the same antenna:

answer.pre: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ R⁴)      or      P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> A<sub>e</sub>² σ / (4π λ² R⁴)

answer: Minimum detectable signal: the receiver noise referred to the input is kT<sub>0</sub>BF. Detection with the wanted P<sub>d</sub> and P<sub>fa</sub> needs the echo to exceed this by (S/N)<sub>min</sub>, so S<sub>min</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>BF(S/N)<sub>min</sub>. System losses L (waveguide, duplexer, radome, processing) divide the echo.

answer.text: Setting P<sub>r</sub>/L = S<sub>min</sub> at R = R<sub>max</sub>:
answer.pre: R<sub>max</sub> = [ P<sub>t</sub> G² λ² σ / ((4π)³ k T<sub>0</sub> B F (S/N)<sub>min</sub> L) ]<sup>1/4</sup>

answer: Dependence: R<sub>max</sub> ∝ P<sub>t</sub><sup>1/4</sup>, G<sup>1/2</sup>, σ<sup>1/4</sup>. Doubling the range needs 16 times the power or 4 times the gain. With G fixed, R<sub>max</sub> ∝ λ<sup>1/2</sup>; with the antenna area fixed (A<sub>e</sub> form), R<sub>max</sub> ∝ λ<sup>−1/2</sup>, because the same dish has more gain at a shorter wavelength.
Consequences: a target of 0.5 m² (one tenth) is seen at 92.0 × 0.1<sup>1/4</sup> = 51.7 km; 16 times the power (4 MW) would be needed to reach 184 km.

answer.text: Effect of single design changes on the 92.0 km result (R<sub>max</sub> varies as the fourth root of P<sub>t</sub>, G², σ and 1/(F·L)):

answer: The table shows why antenna gain is the most valuable term: it acts on both transmit and receive, so 3 dB of gain buys as much range as four times the power.
Assumptions to state: free space with no multipath, the target on the beam axis, a steady σ, single-pulse detection and B ≈ 1/τ. Integrating pulses or a fluctuating target change (S/N)<sub>min</sub>.

bank.q: Define radar cross section. Explain how the RCS of a metal sphere varies with ka in the Rayleigh, resonance and optical regions, and compare the sphere with a flat plate and a corner reflector. Find σ for a sphere of radius 0.5 m at 100 MHz, 1 GHz and 10 GHz.
outline: σ = 4πR²S<sub>s</sub>/S<sub>i</sub>, an equivalent isotropic area, in m² or dBsm
Rayleigh σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴ (∝ 1/λ⁴), resonance peaks near ka = 1, optical πa²
Plate 4πA²/λ² face-on; trihedral 4πa⁴/(3λ²) over a wide angle
Aspect, fluctuation and stealth
answer: Definition: σ = lim<sub>R→∞</sub> 4πR² S<sub>s</sub>/S<sub>i</sub>, where S<sub>i</sub> is the incident power density at the target and S<sub>s</sub> the scattered density back at the radar. It is the area that, intercepting S<sub>i</sub> and reradiating equally in all directions, would give the observed echo. Unit m²; dBsm = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(σ/1 m²).
σ is not the physical area: it depends on shape, aspect, material, polarisation and wavelength.
Sphere: it looks the same from every direction, so it is the calibration standard. The size parameter is ka = 2πa/λ.
Rayleigh region (ka ≪ 1): σ = 9πa²(ka)⁴, so σ ∝ a⁶/λ⁴. Raindrops and insects lie here, which is why rain clutter rises steeply with frequency.
Resonance (Mie) region (ka ≈ 1 to 10): the wave reflected from the front interferes with a creeping wave around the back, so σ/πa² swings; the first and highest peak is 3.65 at ka ≈ 1.
Optical region (ka > 10): σ = πa², the projected area, independent of λ.
The same sphere returns 3.65 times more at 100 MHz than in the optical region: the resonance is why an RCS figure must always name its band.

Flat plate, face-on: every point reflects in phase, so σ = 4πA²/λ². A 0.25 m² plate at 10 GHz gives 4π × 0.0625/9 × 10⁻⁴ = 873 m² (29.4 dBsm), over a thousand times its area, but only within a degree or so of normal incidence.

Corner reflector (trihedral): three mutually perpendicular plates return the wave parallel to its arrival over a wide cone, with σ = 4πa⁴/(3λ²) for edge a. An a = 0.2 m trihedral at 10 GHz gives 4π × 0.0016/(3 × 9 × 10⁻⁴) = 7.4 m². Boats carry them; test ranges calibrate with them.

Real targets: many scatterers add and cancel, so σ fluctuates by 10 to 20 dB with small changes of aspect; detection uses statistical (Swerling) models. Stealth lowers σ by shaping (no faces or right angles toward the radar, hidden engine faces) and absorbing materials.

Closing check: at 100 MHz the Rayleigh formula would give 9π × 0.25 × 1.047⁴ = 8.5 m², three times the true 2.86 m²; at ka ≈ 1 the sphere is already out of the Rayleigh region, so the formula must not be used there.

bank.q: Compare sequential lobing, conical scan and amplitude-comparison monopulse tracking. Explain the monopulse comparator, and find the angle error when Δ = 0.9 V, Σ = 12 V and the slope is 1.5 per degree, with the cross-range offset at 15 km.
outline: Error signal zero on boresight, sign gives side
Sequential lobing: switched squinted beams, (A<sub>1</sub> − A<sub>2</sub>)/(A<sub>1</sub> + A<sub>2</sub>)
Conical scan: rotating squinted beam, modulation depth and phase
Monopulse: four horns, comparator, Σ, Δ<sub>az</sub>, Δ<sub>el</sub>; Δ/Σ
Comparison table; θ = 0.05°, offset 13.1 m
answer: All three make an angle error signal ε ≈ kθ that is zero on the boresight (tracking axis) and changes sign across it; a servo turns the antenna until ε = 0.

Sequential lobing: one feed is switched between two beam positions squinted either side of boresight (and two more for the other plane). ε = (A1 − A2)/(A1 + A2); for example echoes of 1.08 and 0.92 give 0.16/2.00 = 0.08.

Conical scan: one beam, squinted off axis, rotates about the boresight at a few tens of hertz. On axis the echo is steady; off axis it is modulated once per rotation, the depth giving the size of the error and the phase giving the direction.

Amplitude-comparison monopulse: four horns at the focus give four beams squinted into the quadrants. With A top-left, B bottom-left, C top-right, D bottom-right, a comparator of four magic tees or rat-race hybrids forms:

answer.pre:
Σ    = A + B + C + D          (detection, range, reference)
Δ<sub>az</sub> = (A + B) − (C + D)      (left column − right column)
Δ<sub>el</sub> = (A + C) − (B + D)      (top row − bottom row)

answer: Each channel has its own receiver; the angle is read as θ = (Δ/Σ)/k. Dividing by Σ removes the dependence on echo strength, and the phase of Δ relative to Σ (0° or 180°) gives the side.

Why monopulse wins against a fluctuating target: lobing and conical scan compare echoes taken at different times, so a change of σ between them is read as an angle change; monopulse compares beams on the same pulse.
Cross-range offset at 15 km: 0.050° = 8.73 × 10⁻⁴ rad, so x = Rθ = 15 000 × 8.73 × 10⁻⁴ = 13.1 m.
The servo turns the antenna 0.050° toward the side given by the sign of Δ until Δ<sub>az</sub> is zero; the range gate is tracked separately with split early and late gates.
Closing check: with the antenna corrected, Δ = 0 and Δ/Σ = 0 whatever the value of Σ, which is the defining property of boresight.

bank.q: A radar has PRF = 800 Hz, pulse width 2 µs, peak power 2 MW and duplexer recovery time 1 µs. Find the unambiguous range, duty cycle, average power, minimum range and range resolution. A target at 230 km is observed. Where does it appear? If the radar also uses a PRF of 1000 Hz, show how the true range is recovered, and give the range out to which the pair is unambiguous.
outline: R<sub>unamb</sub> = c/(2·PRF) = 187.5 km
d = 0.0016, P<sub>av</sub> = 3.2 kW
R<sub>min</sub> = c(τ + t<sub>rec</sub>)/2 = 450 m; ΔR = 300 m
Apparent 42.5 km at 800 Hz, 80 km at 1000 Hz
Candidate lists meet at 230 km; pair unambiguous to 750 km
answer: Pulse interval: T<sub>r</sub> = 1/800 = 1.25 ms.
Unambiguous range: R<sub>unamb</sub> = cT<sub>r</sub>/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 1.25 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 187 500 m = 187.5 km.
Average power: P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub>d = 2 × 10⁶ × 0.0016 = 3200 W = 3.2 kW.
Minimum range: R<sub>min</sub> = c(τ + t<sub>rec</sub>)/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 3 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 450 m.
Range resolution: ΔR = cτ/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 300 m.

Apparent range at 800 Hz: the echo from 230 km takes 2 × 230 000/3 × 10⁸ = 1.533 ms, which is 1.533 − 1.25 = 0.283 ms after the second pulse; 0.283 ms corresponds to 42.5 km. In range terms, n = 1 and R<sub>app</sub> = 230 − 187.5 = 42.5 km.

answer.text: Timeline at 800 Hz (one row per interval):
answer.pre:
pulse 1 at 0 ms ──────────── pulse 2 at 1.25 ms ──── echo at 1.533 ms
                                  └── 0.283 ms after pulse 2 → shown at 42.5 km

answer: Eclipsing check: an echo is lost if it arrives while a later pulse is being sent or the duplexer is recovering, that is within 3 µs after a pulse, which happens for ranges from n × 187.5 km to n × 187.5 km + 0.45 km. The 230 km echo arrives 283 µs after pulse 2, far outside this, so it is not eclipsed.
Second PRF: at 1000 Hz, R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km, and the same target appears at 230 − 150 = 80 km.

answer.text: Unfolding: list the ranges that fit each reading.

answer: The first range common to both lists is 230 km, the true range.

Range of the pair: the coincidences repeat every least common multiple of 187.5 and 150 km. 187.5 × 4 = 750 and 150 × 5 = 750, so the pair is unambiguous out to 750 km, four times the lower PRF alone.

Design note: the highest single PRF that would place 230 km correctly is c/(2 × 230 000) = 652 Hz, but it would give fewer pulses per beam width and less Doppler coverage; two PRFs keep the higher rate and still resolve the range.
Closing check: a real target at 42.5 km would appear at 42.5 km at both PRFs; only the folded echo moves (42.5 → 80 km) when the PRF changes, which is how operators recognise it.

bank.q: Explain the Doppler effect and the operation of CW and FMCW radar. (a) A 24.15 GHz speed gun watches a car travelling at 72 km/h on a line 30° from the beam. Find the Doppler shift and the speed the gun reads. (b) An FMCW radio altimeter at 4.3 GHz uses a triangular sweep of 100 MHz at f<sub>m</sub> = 100 Hz. Find the beat frequency at a height of 600 m, the up- and down-sweep beats if the aircraft descends at 5 m/s, and the range resolution.
outline: f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ from the phase 4πR/λ
CW radar: mixer, Doppler filter, no range
FMCW: f<sub>b</sub> = 2RΔf/(cT<sub>m</sub>) = 4RΔf·f<sub>m</sub>/c, triangular sweep separates f<sub>d</sub>
(a) f<sub>d</sub> = 2789 Hz, reads 62.4 km/h
(b) f<sub>R</sub> = 80 kHz, f<sub>d</sub> = 143 Hz, beats 79.86 and 80.14 kHz, ΔR = 1.5 m
answer: Doppler effect: the echo from range R lags the transmitter by φ = 4πR/λ. If R changes at the rate −v<sub>r</sub>, the phase changes at 4πv<sub>r</sub>/λ rad/s, which is a frequency shift f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ (positive, higher echo frequency, for a closing target). Only the radial component v<sub>r</sub> = v cos θ counts.

CW radar: an oscillator runs continuously; separate transmit and receive antennas keep the transmitter out of the receiver; a mixer with a transmitter sample gives f<sub>d</sub>, which a filter and counter read. It cannot measure range (no timing mark) and does not see stationary targets.

FMCW radar: the frequency is swept linearly by Δf; the echo, delayed by 2R/c, differs from the transmitter by the beat f<sub>b</sub> = 2RΔf/(cT<sub>m</sub>), where T<sub>m</sub> is one sweep. For a triangular sweep at modulation frequency f<sub>m</sub>, T<sub>m</sub> = 1/(2f<sub>m</sub>), so f<sub>b</sub> = 4RΔf·f<sub>m</sub>/c. For a closing target, f<sub>up</sub> = f<sub>R</sub> − f<sub>d</sub> and f<sub>down</sub> = f<sub>R</sub> + f<sub>d</sub>.
f<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 17.32 / 0.01242 = 2789 Hz. Head-on the shift would be 2 × 20 / 0.01242 = 3220 Hz.
The gun converts f<sub>d</sub> to speed assuming a head-on car: v = f<sub>d</sub>λ/2 = 17.32 m/s = 62.4 km/h. The cosine error always reads low, in the driver's favour.
(b) λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 4.3 × 10⁹ = 0.06977 m; each sweep lasts T<sub>m</sub> = 1/(2 × 100) = 5 ms.
f<sub>R</sub> = 4RΔf·f<sub>m</sub>/c = 4 × 600 × 10⁸ × 100 / 3 × 10⁸ = 80 000 Hz. Check with the other form: 2 × 600 × 10⁸ / (3 × 10⁸ × 5 × 10⁻³) = 80 000 Hz.
Descent at 5 m/s closes the range: f<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 5 / 0.06977 = 143.3 Hz.
Range resolution: ΔR = c/(2Δf) = 3 × 10⁸ / 2 × 10⁸ = 1.5 m.
Closing check: going back from the beats, R = 80 000 × 3 × 10⁸ / (4 × 10⁸ × 100) = 600 m and v = 143.3 × 0.06977/2 = 5.0 m/s, the values given.

bank.q: Explain the delay-line canceller and blind speeds in MTI radar. An L-band MTI radar at 1.3 GHz has PRF = 400 Hz. Find the first three blind speeds, the single- and double-canceller responses for targets at 23.08 m/s and 34.6 m/s, and the first blind speed when the PRF is staggered between 400 Hz and 500 Hz.
outline: Canceller subtracts pulse n − 1 from pulse n per range gate; |H| = 2|sin(πf<sub>d</sub>T<sub>r</sub>)|
Zeros at f<sub>d</sub> = n·PRF; v<sub>b</sub> = nλ·PRF/2 = 46.2, 92.3, 138.5 m/s
Responses 2.00/4.00 and 1.42/2.00
Staggered 5:4 → first blind speed 230.8 m/s
Price of staggering
answer: Principle: fixed clutter returns the same amplitude and phase on every pulse; a moving target's phase advances by 2πf<sub>d</sub>T<sub>r</sub> per pulse. A coherent MTI radar phase-detects each echo against the COHO, and the canceller subtracts, range gate by range gate, the output of the previous pulse (delayed by exactly T<sub>r</sub>) from the present one.

answer.pre:
single:  |H| = 2 |sin(π f<sub>d</sub> T<sub>r</sub>)|
double:  |H| = 4 sin²(π f<sub>d</sub> T<sub>r</sub>)

answer: Both are zero when f<sub>d</sub> = n/T<sub>r</sub> = n·PRF: the target moves a whole number of half-wavelengths between pulses and looks fixed. The blind speeds are v<sub>b</sub> = nλ·PRF/2.

A target at half the first blind speed gets the full gain; the double canceller doubles the peak response (4 against 2) but its notch around zero is wider, so it cuts slow targets more and rejects spread clutter better.

Staggered PRF: T<sub>1</sub> = 2.5 ms, T<sub>2</sub> = 2.0 ms, T<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>2</sub> = 5/4, so a = 5, b = 4. A target is blind only if f<sub>d</sub>T<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>d</sub>T<sub>2</sub> are both whole numbers: f<sub>d</sub> = 5/T<sub>1</sub> = 4/T<sub>2</sub> = 2000 Hz.

First blind speed: v<sub>b</sub> = 2000 × 0.2308 / 2 = 230.8 m/s (831 km/h). Check: the average interval 2.25 ms gives 0.2308/(2 × 2.25 × 10⁻³) = 51.3 m/s, and (a + b)/2 × 51.3 = 4.5 × 51.3 = 230.8 m/s.
At 46.15 m/s (blind at 400 Hz), the 2.0 ms interval gives 2|sin(π × 400 × 0.002)| = 2 sin 144° = 1.18, so the target is no longer lost.

Why not simply raise the PRF? Pushing the first blind speed above 300 m/s at λ = 0.2308 m would need PRF ≥ 2 × 300/0.2308 = 2600 Hz, which cuts the unambiguous range to 3 × 10⁸/(2 × 2600) = 57.7 km, far too short for an L-band surveillance radar. Staggering keeps the low PRF and its long range.
Price: the response between blind speeds is uneven, clutter cancellation is slightly poorer because the clutter samples are unequally spaced, and the timing and processing are more complex.
Closing check: L band suffers badly from blind speeds because λ is long; at 400 Hz an aircraft at 166 km/h, an ordinary approach speed, would vanish without staggering.

bank.q: A radar receiver has a noise bandwidth of 2 MHz and a noise figure of 3 dB. (a) Find the noise power. (b) Find the square-law threshold for P<sub>fa</sub> = 10⁻⁶ with known noise, and the CA-CFAR multiplier with 24 training cells. (c) An echo of 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ W arrives as a 20 µs linear FM pulse sweeping 2 MHz. Find the input S/N, the matched-filter E/N<sub>0</sub> and 2E/N<sub>0</sub>, the compression ratio and the range resolution.
outline: N = kT<sub>0</sub>BF = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁴ W (−108.0 dBm)
τB = 40 (16.0 dB); ΔR = 75 m against 3 km uncoded
answer: (b) Known noise: a square-law detector sees noise power with an exponential distribution of mean μ, so P<sub>fa</sub> = exp(−T/μ). T/μ = −ln 10⁻⁶ = 13.82: the threshold sits 13.82 times (11.4 dB) above the mean noise power.
CA-CFAR: the noise is estimated as the mean Z of N = 24 training cells and the threshold is αZ, with P<sub>fa</sub> = (1 + α/N)<sup>−N</sup>.

Check: (1 + 18.68/24)<sup>−24</sup> = 1.778<sup>−24</sup> = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶. The CFAR threshold is 18.68/13.82 = 1.352 times, or 1.31 dB, above the known-noise value; this is roughly the CFAR loss, the price of not knowing the noise level exactly.
(c) Input S/N in the 2 MHz bandwidth: 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 0.626 (−2.0 dB). Before compression the echo is below the noise.
Energy: E = P<sub>r</sub>τ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Noise density: N<sub>0</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>F = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 1.995 = 7.99 × 10⁻²¹ W/Hz.
Matched-filter output: E/N<sub>0</sub> = 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 7.99 × 10⁻²¹ = 25.0 (14.0 dB) on the average-power basis, and 2E/N<sub>0</sub> = 50.1 (17.0 dB) on the peak-power basis.

Why the CFAR is needed: if rain raises the background 10 dB, a fixed threshold set at 13.82 times the receiver noise sits only 1.382 times above the new mean, and P<sub>fa</sub> = exp(−1.382) = 0.25, a false alarm in every fourth cell. The CA-CFAR threshold αZ rises with Z, so P<sub>fa</sub> stays at 10⁻⁶ (as long as the training cells see the same rain).

Decision: a steady target needs about 13.1 dB of single-pulse S/N for P<sub>d</sub> = 0.9 at P<sub>fa</sub> = 10⁻⁶ (Albersheim's estimate), so the compressed echo at 14.0 dB would usually be detected, while the uncompressed −2.0 dB echo would almost never be.
Closing check: the S/N gain of the matched filter equals the time-bandwidth product, 0.626 × 40 = 25.0, as it must for a chirp whose bandwidth equals the receiver bandwidth.

bank.q: Explain the branch-type duplexer with TR and ATR tubes and the need for a receiver protector. A 9.4 GHz radar has 500 kW peak power, a receiver that can take 50 mW, a 1 µs pulse, a TR recovery time of 2 µs and a PRF of 2 kHz, with a 3 m dish of efficiency 0.6. Find the isolation needed, the minimum range, the average power, the beamwidth and the gain.
outline: TR tube in the receiver arm, ATR in the transmitter arm, quarter-wave spacings
Transmit and receive states
Leading-edge spike and recovery; limiter
I = 70 dB; R<sub>min</sub> = 450 m; P<sub>av</sub> = 1 kW
answer: Layout: the transmitter, antenna and receiver meet at a junction. The TR tube sits in the receiver arm and the ATR tube in a side arm of the transmitter line, each placed a quarter wavelength from the junction.

Transmit: the high-power pulse fires both gas tubes. The fired TR tube is a short circuit across the receiver arm, which the quarter-wave line turns into an open circuit at the junction, so no power enters the receiver arm and the receiver is shielded. The fired ATR tube is a short at the end of a quarter-wave stub, which looks like an open across the main line and lets the pulse pass to the antenna.

Receive: the weak echo cannot fire either tube. The unfired ATR arm now presents a short a quarter wave from the junction, which appears as an open there and blocks the transmitter arm; the echo goes into the receiver.
A balanced duplexer uses two 3 dB hybrids and two TR tubes for more power and bandwidth; a ferrite circulator with a limiter does the same job in modern sets.

Receiver protection: at the start of each pulse the gas takes a short time to ionise, so a spike leaks through that is larger than the steady leakage; after the pulse the TR tube needs time to deionise (recovery). A diode limiter after the duplexer clips the spike.

Reading the numbers: a TR tube alone gives about 60 to 70 dB, so it barely meets the 70 dB and the limiter is essential. The recovery time costs 300 m of the 450 m blind zone, more than the pulse itself.
The 0.74° beam at 47.2 dB gain suits a precision or marine radar; the waveguide and duplexer must stand 500 kW peak, while the cooling handles only 1 kW.
Closing check: 10⁷ in power is 70 dB, and +87 − 70 = +17 dBm = 50 mW, exactly the receiver limit, so any extra leakage (the spike) would exceed it.

bank.q: Design outline: an airport surveillance radar must detect a 1 m² aircraft at 100 km with a 1.5° azimuth beam. Choose and justify the band, the PRF and the pulse width. At 2.8 GHz, with an antenna efficiency of 0.6, B = 1 MHz, F = 3 dB, (S/N)<sub>min</sub> = 13 dB and system loss 8 dB, find the antenna size, the gain and the peak power needed, and comment on the result.
outline: S band: little rain loss, a 5 m antenna; L band too big, X band too lossy
PRF ≤ 1.25 kHz for 120 km; 1 kHz gives 150 km; τ = 1 µs for 150 m
S<sub>min</sub> = 1.59 × 10⁻¹³ W; P<sub>t</sub> = 104 kW, P<sub>av</sub> = 104 W
Comment: integration of about 20 hits per scan, fluctuating target, real fan beam
answer: Band: an airport radar must see through heavy rain near the airport and fit on a tower. X band would need only a 1.5 m antenna but loses badly in monsoon rain and sees strong rain clutter; L band would need a 10.8 m antenna for 1.5°. S band (2.7 to 2.9 GHz) needs about 5 m and passes rain well, so it is the standard choice.

PRF: echoes must return before the next pulse from a little beyond the 100 km requirement, say 120 km: PRF ≤ c/(2 × 120 000) = 1250 Hz. Choose 1000 Hz, giving R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km, with staggering to move the blind speeds out.
Pulse width: aircraft on approach must be separated by well under a kilometre: τ = 1 µs gives ΔR = 150 m and matches B = 1 MHz.
Gain (treating it as a pencil beam): G = η(πD/λ)² = 0.6 × (π × 5 / 0.1071)² = 0.6 × 21 494 = 12 896 = 41.1 dB.
Minimum detectable signal: kT<sub>0</sub>BF = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 10⁶ × 1.995 = 7.98 × 10⁻¹⁵ W; × (S/N)<sub>min</sub> 19.95 gives S<sub>min</sub> = 1.59 × 10⁻¹³ W (−128.0 dBW).

answer.text: Range equation solved for P<sub>t</sub>, in dB:

answer: P<sub>t</sub> = 10<sup>5.019</sup> = 104 500 W ≈ 104 kW peak. Average power at 1 µs and 1000 Hz: 104 kW × 0.001 = 104 W.

Hits per scan: at 12 rpm the antenna turns 72°/s, so it dwells 1.5/72 = 0.021 s on a target and collects about 21 pulses. Integrating them lowers the S/N needed per pulse by several dB (up to 21 times coherently), so a few tens of kilowatts would do in practice.

Margins to add: a fluctuating aircraft echo needs several dB more S/N for a high P<sub>d</sub>; the real antenna is a fan beam (narrow in azimuth, broad cosecant-squared in elevation), whose gain is lower than the pencil-beam 41.1 dB; and rain loss at long range.

Transmitter choice: 100 kW at 0.1 % duty is easy for a klystron, a TWT or a solid-state transmitter with pulse compression; a coherent source is needed because MTI is essential against ground clutter around an airport.

bank.q: Compare CW, FMCW, low-PRF pulse and pulse Doppler radar for measuring range and radial speed. For an X-band radar (λ = 3 cm) that must measure closing speeds up to 300 m/s without Doppler ambiguity, find the PRF needed and the resulting unambiguous range, and explain how medium-PRF radars resolve the conflict.
outline: CW speed only; FMCW range and speed; low PRF range; pulse Doppler speed
f<sub>d</sub> = 20 kHz at 300 m/s; ±f<sub>d</sub> needs PRF ≥ 40 kHz; R<sub>unamb</sub> = 3.75 km
Low PRF 1 kHz: Doppler span only 15 m/s
Medium PRF and several PRFs; trade-off table
answer: CW radar: measures radial speed precisely from fd; no range, no stationary targets. Simple and low power: speed guns, intruder alarms.

FMCW radar: a linear sweep gives range from the beat, and a triangular sweep gives speed as well; low peak power, fine resolution c/(2Δf), but short range and strong transmitter leakage: altimeters, level gauges, car radar.
Low-PRF pulse radar: measures range unambiguously over a long distance; Doppler is sampled only at the PRF, so speed is ambiguous. Search and air traffic radars, with MTI for clutter.
Pulse Doppler radar: a high or medium PRF and a Doppler filter bank measure speed and reject clutter; range is ambiguous and resolved with several PRFs. Airborne fire-control radars.
Doppler needed: f<sub>d</sub> = 2v<sub>r</sub>/λ = 2 × 300 / 0.03 = 20 000 Hz.

Unambiguous Doppler: phase samples once per pulse can tell Doppler frequencies apart only over a span of one PRF. To measure both closing and opening targets up to ±20 kHz the span must be 40 kHz: PRF ≥ 40 kHz (20 kHz would do for closing targets only).
Unambiguous range at 40 kHz: c/(2 × 40 000) = 3750 m = 3.75 km, useless for search on its own.
At a low PRF of 1 kHz the unambiguous range is 150 km, but the Doppler span of 1000 Hz covers only 1000 × 0.03/2 = 15 m/s of speed, so a 300 m/s target folds many times.

Medium PRF: the radar cycles through several PRFs near 10 kHz (for example three of a set of eight). Each is ambiguous in both range and Doppler, but only mildly, and the true range and the true speed are the single values consistent with all the readings, as with two PRFs in range unfolding. Blind zones in range and speed differ from PRF to PRF, so a target hidden in one is seen in another.
Choice: a ground speed gun is CW; a car radar that must see a stopped car is FMCW; an airport search radar is low PRF with MTI; a fighter radar uses medium and high PRF pulse Doppler.
Closing check: at PRF 40 kHz, a 300 m/s target's 20 kHz shift is exactly half the PRF, the edge of the unambiguous span ±PRF/2, consistent with the requirement.

bank.q: Evaluate pulse compression. A radar with 1 MW peak power uses a 1 µs uncoded pulse. It is replaced by a 20 µs linear FM pulse of 1 MHz bandwidth at the same peak power, and then by the same chirp at 50 kW peak. Compare the pulse energy, S/N, detection range, range resolution and average power (PRF 1 kHz) in the three cases, and state the costs of compression.
outline: Matched filter S/N depends on E = P<sub>t</sub>τ
Chirp at 1 MW: 20 × energy, +13 dB, range × 2.11, resolution still 150 m
Chirp at 50 kW: same energy and range as the short pulse at 1/20 of the peak power
Average power 1 kW, 20 kW, 1 kW
Costs: range sidelobes, longer blind zone, Doppler mismatch, processing
answer: Principle: the matched-filter output S/N is 2E/N<sub>0</sub>, set by the pulse energy E = P<sub>t</sub>τ, not by the shape. Range resolution is set by the bandwidth, c/(2B). An uncoded pulse ties the two together (B ≈ 1/τ); a chirp breaks the tie by sweeping B over a long τ, and its matched filter compresses it to about 1/B.

Same peak power: the chirp has 20 times the energy, so 10 log<sub>10</sub> 20 = 13.0 dB more S/N, and the range grows as the fourth root: 20<sup>1/4</sup> = 2.11 times, with the same 150 m resolution. But the average power rises to 20 kW, which the transmitter and cooling must supply.

Same energy: at 50 kW the chirp matches the detection range of the 1 MW short pulse. This is why solid-state transmitters, whose modules give modest peak power, depend on pulse compression: they trade peak power for pulse length.

Costs: (1) the compressed pulse has range sidelobes about 13 dB down for a plain chirp, which can hide a small target next to a large one, so a weighting window is used at the cost of a slightly wider main lobe and about 1 dB of S/N; (2) the long pulse blinds the receiver for longer, here 3 km instead of 150 m, so a short pulse is often added to cover close range; (3) a Doppler shift moves the compressed peak slightly in range (range-Doppler coupling); (4) the matched filter needs more processing, now cheap in digital form.
Verdict: compression is worth it whenever peak power is limited or resolution must be fine at long range; it is used in nearly every modern surveillance and tracking radar.

Closing check: compression ratio τB = 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁶ = 20, the same factor as the energy ratio at equal peak power, and the S/N gain of the matched filter over the input S/N in a 1 MHz bandwidth is also 20 (13.0 dB).

glossary.def: The horizontal angle of a target, measured from a reference direction such as north.
The angle of a target above the horizontal.
The tracking axis of an antenna: the direction in which its angle error signal is zero.
Unwanted echoes from ground, sea, rain, birds or other objects that are not targets.
The time between the starts of two successive pulses, T<sub>r</sub> = 1/PRF.
The fraction of time the transmitter is on, τ/T<sub>r</sub> = τ·PRF.
A time window, one pulse width long, that selects the echoes from one small band of range.
An echo from beyond the unambiguous range that arrives after the next pulse and is shown too close.
Changing the pulse interval from pulse to pulse so that blind speeds move out and second-time-around echoes jump about.
A radial speed at which the Doppler shift is a multiple of the PRF, so an MTI canceller removes the target.
An MTI filter that subtracts the previous pulse's output from the present one, range gate by range gate.
The output signal-to-clutter ratio of an MTI divided by the input ratio, averaged over target speeds.
Coherent oscillator: the IF phase reference against which each echo is phase-detected in a coherent radar.
Stable local oscillator: the low-noise oscillator that drives the receiver mixer.
In monopulse, the sum of the four beams: a normal beam used for detection and range.
In monopulse, the difference of beam pairs: zero on boresight, with a sign that gives the side.
Tracking by rotating a squinted beam about the boresight and reading the echo modulation.
Tracking by switching between squinted beams and comparing their echoes.
The filter whose impulse response is the time-reversed pulse; it gives the highest peak S/N in white noise.
A detector whose threshold follows a local estimate of the background, so the false-alarm probability stays fixed.
The probability that noise alone crosses the threshold in one cell.
Sending a long coded pulse and compressing it in the receiver, giving the energy of a long pulse with the resolution of a short one.
An elevation pattern whose gain falls as csc²θ above the horizon, giving a steady echo from a target at constant height.
The switch that lets one antenna serve the transmitter and the receiver while protecting the receiver.
A gas tube that fires during the pulse and shorts the receiver branch of a duplexer.
A ferrite three-port device that passes power from port to port in one direction only.
Plan position indicator: a map display with range out from the centre and azimuth around it.
A cover over an antenna that must be transparent in the radar band.
